w2: Before you act on a painful thought, take a small sample and test it, the way a surgeon tests tissue before operating.
w3: Catch the thought and write it down in a few words
w4: Ask: "Is it true?" What is the evidence for and against it?
w5: Ask: "Is it helpful?" Does it move me toward love and wise action?
w6: Ask: "Does it fit who God says I am and who I want to become?"
w7: If it fails the test, write one true replacement and say it out loud
w9: Start with feelings: when your mood drops, ask "What was I just thinking?"
w11: Feelings are not proof; look for the facts a fair friend would see
w13: Do one biopsy every evening on the loudest thought of the day
w14: Automatic thoughts run along well-worn pathways. Stopping to examine one brings the prefrontal cortex online and stops feeding the old circuit; choosing a truer thought again and again strengthens a new one (cognitive restructuring and neuroplasticity).
w15: When a bad thought comes, check it like a doctor: Is it true? Does it help? Does it fit what God says about me? If not, swap it for a true one.
w18: A one-minute reset for your mind in three letters: Curious, Perform a quick biopsy, Replace.
w19: C, get Curious: pause and ask, "What am I thinking and feeling right now?"
w20: P, Perform a quick biopsy: "Is this true, and does it need a response right now?"
w21: R, Replace it: say one true sentence, such as "I am safe right now" or "God is with me"
w22: Breathe out slowly once and choose your next action
w23: In the moment my mind goes blank
w24: Just remember the three letters C, P, R
w26: Repeat the reset; each repeat weakens the old path
w27: I don't know what is true
w28: Use a verse you know by heart as your replacement
w29: Curiosity moves the brain from threat mode into exploring mode. Naming and questioning a thought calms the amygdala, and rehearsing a replacement trains a new response.
w30: In one minute: wonder what you are thinking, check if it is true, and say something true instead.
w33: When you feel triggered, give your thinking brain a few seconds with one slow breath before you speak or act.
w34: Notice the trigger in your body: heat, a tight chest, a clenched jaw
w35: Breathe in for about two seconds and out for about three
w37: Ask: "What do I want to happen here?"
w38: Then respond, or say "Give me a minute"
w40: Choose one body warning sign to watch for this week
w42: Take a 20-minute break and come back
w44: Say: "I want to answer well. Give me a moment."
w45: The alarm system reacts in a fraction of a second, while the prefrontal cortex is quieter and takes a few seconds to come online. A brief pause and a long out-breath give the wiser brain time to catch up (amygdala hijack and the vagal brake).
w46: When you get upset, take one slow breath before you talk. It gives your wise brain time to wake up.
w49: Hope is the first medicine any healing plan needs. Practise it in three parts: remember, trust, move.
w50: Remember: write down one time God helped you or things got better
w51: Trust: read one promise of God and say, "This is for me too"
w52: Move: choose one small action that hope would take today
w54: Tonight, note one sign of progress, even a tiny one
w55: I feel no hope at all
w56: Borrow hope: ask a friend to hope and pray for you until you can
w57: The promises feel like they are for other people
w58: Read them aloud with your own name in them
w59: I can't think of a good memory
w60: Start with today: one thing that was not as bad as it could have been
w61: Hope is not only a feeling; it is remembering, expecting and acting. Expecting good engages the brain's motivation circuits, and each small step gives the brain evidence that change is possible. People with more hope are more likely to keep going with treatment.
w62: Hope is like the first medicine. Remember when God helped you, believe He will help again, and take one small step.
w63: Name the Wound in One Sentence
w65: Write exactly what happened and exactly what you felt, in one honest sentence, as a first step in healing an old hurt.
w67: Write one sentence: "What happened was… and I felt…"
w68: Read it slowly and breathe out
w69: Offer the sentence to God: "Lord, this is what happened, and this is how it felt"
w70: When you are ready, share it with one safe person or a counsellor
w72: Write only the first half today, or stop and use a grounding tool
w74: Write what happened, not what you think it says about you
w76: That is common at first; keep it short and end with something soothing
w77: Putting a painful experience into clear words helps the brain store it as a memory rather than an ongoing threat, and naming feelings calms the amygdala (affect labelling and expressive writing research).
w78: Write one sentence about what hurt you and how you felt. Telling God and a safe person helps the hurt heal.
w81: When you feel stuck, change one small thing on purpose today. Nothing changes until something changes.
w82: Name where you feel stuck in one sentence
w83: Notice the usual pattern: the time, the place, the thought and the action
w84: Change one small part of it: a different time, route, first sentence or response
w85: Pray: "Lord, lead me in a new way"
w86: Write down what happened, and do it again tomorrow
w87: I don't know what to change
w88: Change the first five minutes of your morning
w90: You are not aiming for perfection, only interruption
w91: I slip back into the old way
w92: Every interruption still weakens the old path
w93: When we feel stuck, the brain is replaying familiar patterns on autopilot, often through the default mode network. A deliberate change, however small, breaks the cue-and-routine chain and starts laying down a new pathway.
w94: When you feel stuck, do one small thing differently today. Small changes start to make new paths in your brain.
w97: Give grief a little time each day, with God, so it can move instead of getting stuck.
w99: Look at a photo, or write about the person or thing you lost
w100: Let yourself feel it, and cry if you need to
w101: Tell God honestly what you miss
w102: Finish with something kind for your body: a walk, a warm drink or a rest
w103: I'm afraid I won't stop crying
w104: Set a timer and end with a soothing activity
w105: It has been a long time and nothing is lifting
w106: Talk to a counsellor; prolonged grief can be helped
w107: People say I should be over it
w108: Grief has no deadline; love goes on
w109: Losing someone we are attached to activates some of the same circuits as physical pain. Grief is not a problem to solve but love adjusting to a loss; giving it regular space, with support, helps the brain slowly update its map of the world.
w110: When you miss someone very much, give the sadness a little time each day and tell God about it. Slowly, the pain gets softer.
w111: After the 40 Days: Who Are You Now?
w113: At the end of a season of prayer or change, look back, name who you are becoming and choose what comes next.
w114: Read back through your notes from the season
w115: Write three ways you have changed, however small
w116: Ask God: "Who are You making me to be?" and write what comes to mind that agrees with Scripture
w117: Choose one practice to keep going
w118: Tell someone what God has done
w120: Ask a close friend what they have noticed
w121: I feel I failed the season
w122: Count the days you showed up, not the days you missed
w123: I don't know what is next
w124: Keep one simple daily rhythm for the next 40 days
w125: Reflecting on progress strengthens new identity and motivation; the brain remembers what we review. Naming who we are becoming helps new habits last beyond the first push.
w126: After a time of praying or changing, look back and see how you have grown. Then choose one good thing to keep doing.
w127: Self-Brain Surgery: Operating on Your Thoughts
w128: A neurosurgeon's picture for renewing the mind: diagnose the thought, prepare your body, operate by replacing it, then let the new pathway heal and grow.
